input.command:
gh pr create --title "test: pin down checkpoint push behavior for multi-push-URL remotes" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## What

A single git remote can carry several push URLs — `remote.<name>.pushurl` may repeat, and a repeated `remote.<name>.url` has the same effect. It's how people mirror to two forges in one push, or keep a backup remote. Verified behavior:

| Config | Fetch | Push |
|---|---|---|
| `remote.origin.url` ×2 | uses only the **first** | goes to **both** |
| `remote.origin.pushurl` ×2 | uses `url` | goes to **both** pushurls |

Two git facts drive everything here:

1. `git push origin` fans out to **every** push URL.
2. git invokes the pre-push hook **once per push URL**, passing the same remote *name* as `$1` each time and the individual URL as `$2`.

Our installed hook forwards only `$1` (`strategy/hooks.go`), so the CLI sees N identical invocations and hands `git push <name>` the name — letting git fan out a second time. It has no per-URL control at all: it can decide *whether* to push checkpoints for an invocation, not *where* they land.

This PR adds integration coverage for what that means, and is **tests only** — no production change.

## Bugs documented

Both use the existing `t.Skip("KNOWN BUG: …")` convention (see `remote_operations_test.go:625`), placed so everything above the skip still enforces what works today, and the assertions *after* it state the desired behavior. Fixing either is a one-line deletion.

**1. Divergence recovery only ever reconciles the fetch URL.** When push URLs diverge independently, the rejected push triggers fetch+rebase recovery — but `git fetch <remote>` reads only the remote's fetch URL. URL A converges; URL B is left rejected with its divergence unmergeable. Captured hook output:

```
[entire] Pushing entire/checkpoints/v1 to origin...          ← rejected by both
[entire] Syncing entire/checkpoints/v1 with remote... done    ← fetched from URL A only
[entire] Pushing entire/checkpoints/v1 to origin...           ← retry
[entire] Warning: failed to push entire/checkpoints/v1 after sync: non-fast-forward
```

`git push` exits **0**, so this is silent: the second mirror just stops receiving checkpoints, and the only trace is a warning that doesn't name the URL that rejected it. It also can't self-heal within the push — there is one remote-tracking ref per remote *name*, and git advances it to the hash the *successful* URL accepted, so `pushRefIfNeeded`'s up-to-date check reports "in sync with origin" and the second hook invocation short-circuits. That mechanism is logged rather than asserted.

**2. Adding a push URL defeats the empty-remote guard.** `deferCheckpointPushOnEmptyRemote` exists because `entire/checkpoints/v1` is a real `refs/heads` branch a forge would adopt as the default branch of an empty repo. The guard asks whether the remote *name* has local remote-tracking refs — it does, thanks to the established first URL — so it permits the push, and the fan-out publishes v1 into a brand-new second URL that has no branches. The hook runs before git transfers the user's branch, so v1 gets there first.

## Passing coverage

- `..._Branch_FanOutToBothPushURLs` / `..._Refs_FanOutToBothPushURLs` — both URLs receive checkpoints, on both backends.
- `..._Branch_RepeatedPushesKeepBothURLsInSync` — three sequential checkpoints, both URLs in sync with identical v1 tips. This is the property a mirror user depends on, and exists to fail loudly if checkpoint pushes are ever retargeted at a single resolved URL. That looks like a tidy way to serve a user who *doesn't* want checkpoints mirrored, but it silently breaks the user who configured several push URLs precisely because they do. A single destination must come from explicit config, never be inferred from topology.
- `..._Refs_UnreachableSecondPushURL_RefsStayQueued` — git-refs leaves refs queued after a partially failed push instead of dropping them, so later pushes retry. This is the concrete behavioral difference from the git-branch path, which drops the failure on the floor.

An unreachable URL rather than divergence is used for the git-refs failure case on purpose: per-checkpoint refs only fast-forward and an ID is minted once, so same-ref divergence isn't reachable without a backfill or migration rewriting an existing checkpoint.

## Notes for reviewers

- `AddSecondPushURL` re-adds the remote's original URL as an explicit `pushurl` before adding the new one. Configuring *any* `pushurl` replaces `url` for push purposes, so adding only the new one silently redirects instead of fanning out. The helper asserts it ended up with two.
- Both fan-out helpers re-baseline the `.git/config` guard, since changing push URLs is deliberate.
- The negative assertions aren't vacuous — the fan-out baselines prove the second URL *does* receive checkpoints on the happy path.

## Test plan

- `go test -tags=integration -run TestMultiPushURL ./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/` — 4 pass, 2 skip
- Full integration package green; `mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean
- Unrelated pre-existing flake seen while validating: a spawned subprocess intermittently segfaults under `-race` (~1 in 3 full-package runs), hitting a different test each time. Reproduced with these files removed from the tree, so it predates this branch.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

gh pr create --title "fix(checkpoint): base checkpoint_remote ownership on origin, not the push target" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## Background: what the fork check was for

`checkpoint_remote` is normally committed in `.entire/settings.json`, so anyone who forks a project inherits it. `e8b589835` added "fork detection" to stop a contributor's session data being pushed into the upstream project's checkpoint repo — one they typically can't write to and shouldn't be writing to. Sound guard.

It was implemented by comparing **the push remote's** owner to the checkpoint repo's owner.

## The problem

That conflates two different questions: *"is this `checkpoint_remote` mine?"* and *"where is this particular push going?"* Two consequences:

- **Pushing to any differently-owned remote disables your own `checkpoint_remote`** — and the fallback then sends the checkpoints *to that remote*. A backup remote in another org, or a colleague's fork, receives your session transcripts instead of your configured checkpoint repo. Exactly the opposite of what the explicit setting asked for.
- **It cannot be expressed at all for a remote with several push URLs.** git allows `remote.<name>.pushurl` to repeat and pushes to all of them, so one boolean verdict has to cover a set of destinations that may have different owners.

Nothing in the suite pinned the intended reading: 16 of 18 `TestPushURL` cases use `pushRemote: "origin"`, and the two `"upstream"` cases exercise a *missing* remote rather than a differently-owned one. "Push remote owner" and "origin owner" were indistinguishable everywhere.

## The fix

Ask the ownership question directly, from two local signals — no network, so the pre-push path stays free of SSH passphrase/security-key prompts:

1. A `checkpoint_remote` in `.entire/settings.local.json` is gitignored and per-clone, so it **cannot** have been inherited by cloning or forking. Always ours.
2. Otherwise compare the checkpoint repo's owner against **origin's** owner: *"am I working in a repo owned by whoever owns the checkpoint repo?"* A fork clone has origin `<fork>/app` against an upstream-owned checkpoint repo, and mismatches.

The push destination no longer enters the decision, which is what makes the multi-push-URL case expressible at all.

**Both existing fork tests pass unchanged** — they were written with `originURL` set to the fork (`https://github.com/fork/app.git`, `entire://.../gh/fork/app`), which is good evidence this is the reading that was intended all along.

Signal 1 doubles as the escape hatch for a checkpoint repo legitimately owned by a different account or org than origin — a config the previous check had no way to express.

## Also in here

- **Read the push remote's URL with `git remote get-url --push`** when deriving transport. A remote's push destination is `remote.<name>.pushurl` when set, so the plain `url` can name a different repository than the one being pushed to. Latent until now because `url == pushurl` in the common case.
- **The inherited case logs at Warn instead of Debug**, with the `settings.local.json` hint, so a user whose `checkpoint_remote` is being ignored can find out why.

## Behavior changes

| Scenario | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Fork clone, inherited committed setting | ignored, checkpoints → your remote | unchanged |
| Own repo, push to a differently-owned remote | **ignored, checkpoints → that remote** | honored, checkpoints → checkpoint repo |
| `checkpoint_remote` in `settings.local.json`, origin owner differs | ignored | honored |
| Remote with a `pushurl` in another repo | transport from the fetch url | transport from the push url |
| Origin absent / non-forge URL (local paths) | fallback | unchanged |

## Not in scope

Divergence recovery across multiple push URLs is a separate problem with its own constraint (fast-forward-only push plus one local ref cannot satisfy N independently diverged remotes with cherry-pick reconciliation). It's documented with executable specs in #1897 and needs its own design.

## Test plan

- Three new `TestPushURL` cases, each verified to fail against the previous implementation: differently-owned push remote with matching origin; `settings.local.json` provenance; transport derived from the push URL. Reverting just the `GetPushURL` call makes the last one fail with `https://…` where `git@…` is expected.
- All pre-existing `TestPushURL` cases pass unchanged.
- `go test -tags=integration -race -count=1 ./...` green; `mise run test:e2e:canary` 4/4; `mise run fmt && mise run lint` clean.
- README and `docs/testing/git-remote-test-plan.md` (row B5) updated to describe ownership by origin, including the two cases that must *not* fall back.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF

I found relevant information about this issue. Here's a summary of the search results:

## Race Detector Issues with fork() on Darwin

The search results reveal several related issues in Go concerning the interaction between the race detector and fork/exec operations on macOS (Darwin):

### The Core Problem

RawSyscall is used in a variety of rather unsafe conditions, such as after fork in forkAndExecInChild, and race instrumentation is disabled to avoid calling TSAN in unsafe conditions.

### Issues on macOS Monterey and Later

Multiple GitHub issues document SIGABRT and SIGSEGV crashes when running code with the race detector (`-race` flag) on macOS Monterey that involve `forkAndExecInChild`:

- SIGABRT crashes occurring in the `syscall.rawSyscall` function within `forkAndExecInChild` when the race detector is enabled
- Memory allocation errors and SIGABRT crashes when building with `-race` on MacOS Monterey 12.1 when using the os/exec package

### The Solution

The calls to rawSyscall are okay because they are assembly functions that do not grow the stack, and the `//go:norace` directive is applied to `forkAndExecInChild` to prevent race detector instrumentation.

The fundamental issue is that the race detector instrumentation cannot safely be applied to code that executes after a fork() call, as the child process inherits a corrupted state of TSAN (ThreadSanitizer).

content.text:
Found it. It's a Go toolchain bug on darwin, not our code.

## The chain

The macOS crash report (`integration_test.test-*.ips`, timestamped to my exact failing runs) says `crashed on child side of fork pre-exec` — SIGSEGV at `0x8`, single-threaded child, parent `integration_test.test`. Symbolizing the frames:

```
os/exec.(*Cmd).CombinedOutput → Run → Start → os.StartProcess → os.startProcess
  → syscall.forkExec → syscall.forkAndExecInChild
    → syscall.rawSyscall
      → __tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl(__tsan::ThreadState*)   ← SIGSEGV
```

The forked child reaches the **ThreadSanitizer runtime** before it execs. TSan is not fork-safe — its trace buffer and locks were copied mid-flight from the multithreaded parent — so the child dies. That's why the "subprocess failure" produced no output and why `entire`/`git` are irrelevant: neither ever ran.

## Why the child is instrumented at all

`syscall.forkAndExecInChild` is `//go:norace`, and its comment says:

> In the child, this function must not acquire any locks… **The calls to rawSyscall are okay because they are assembly functions** that do not grow the stack.

That's false on darwin. Because Go routes syscalls through libSystem, `rawSyscall`/`rawSyscall6`/`rawSyscall9` in `syscall/syscall_darwin.go` are ordinary **Go functions** wrapping libc trampolines, carrying `//go:nosplit` and `//go:uintptrkeepalive` — but **not `//go:norace`**.

Linux has exactly that pragma, for exactly this reason (`syscall/syscall_linux.go`):

> `//go:norace`, on RawSyscall, to avoid race instrumentation **if RawSyscall is called after fork**, or from a signal handler.

So the protection Linux added is missing on the darwin path. Confirmed on go1.26.4 / macOS 26.6 / arm64; it's a known upstream class ([#49138](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/49138), [#50172](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50172), [#50323](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50323)).

## Why it looks so random

`TraceSwitchPartImpl` only runs when TSan's trace-buffer *part boundary* is hit, so the crash needs that boundary to fall inside the child's handful of instrumented events. Hence a low, load-dependent rate, and a different victim test each time. It also explains two negative results along the way: a minimal fork/exec storm doesn't reproduce it even under `-race` (its workers do no instrumented memory work), and six standalone runs of the compiled race binary were clean — the earlier failures happened under heavier load.

## Scope, and what I'd do

**CI is unaffected** — `ci.yml` runs `ubuntu-latest`, where the pragma exists. This only costs local macOS developers time, which is presumably why it's gone unfixed.

The mitigation I'd suggest is sharper than "tolerate the flake": **don't run `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test` under `-race` at all.** That package's subject is a *spawned* `entire` binary, and TestMain builds it with a plain `go build` — no `-race`. So `-race` there instruments only the test harness and **cannot detect races in the CLI under test**. It's paying flakiness for essentially zero coverage. Keep `-race` for the unit packages, where the code under test actually runs in-process.

That's a one-line change to `test:ci`, but it does reduce what CI nominally checks, so I'd rather you decide than have me slip it into an unrelated PR. The other half is a genuine 3-line upstream fix — add `//go:norace` to darwin's `rawSyscall`, `rawSyscall6`, `rawSyscall9` — which is worth filing with the Linux comment as precedent, and is small enough to contribute.

Memory updated with the root cause so the next person doesn't re-derive it. Want me to do the `test:ci` split, file the upstream issue, or both?

This runs unit tests, integration tests, and the E2E canary (Vogon agent) in sequence. Integration tests use the `//go:build integration` build tag and are located in `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`. It delegates to the same tasks CI runs (`test:ci:core`, then integration shards `a`/`b`/`c`, then the canary), so a local pass matches CI.

**`-race` is deliberately off for the integration package on darwin.** ThreadSanitizer is not fork-safe there: `syscall.rawSyscall` on darwin is a Go function lacking `//go:norace` (Linux's `RawSyscall` carries it precisely "to avoid race instrumentation if RawSyscall is called after fork"), so under `-race` the instrumentation runs in the child of `fork()` before `exec` and intermittently segfaults it. It surfaces as `signal: segmentation fault` from a spawned subprocess, on a random test, roughly one run in three — indistinguishable from a real regression until you read `~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/integration_test.test-*.ips`. See golang/go#49138. The gate lives in `mise-tasks/test/ci/integration/shard`; do not re-add `-race` there. CI runs Linux, where the pragma exists, so its race coverage is unchanged. Note also that this package is overwhelmingly subprocess-driven — the spawned binary is built without `-race`, so `-race` here can only ever instrument the test harness, not the CLI under test.

gh pr create --title "test: stop running the integration package under -race on darwin" --body "$(cat <<'EOF'
## The bug

`go test -tags=integration -race ./...` intermittently fails on macOS with `signal: segmentation fault` from a spawned subprocess — a **different test each run**, roughly 1 in 3 full-package runs, with no output and no Go panic. It looks exactly like a real regression in whatever change you happen to be working on.

It isn't. It's the Go toolchain on darwin.

The macOS crash report (`~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/integration_test.test-*.ips`) says `crashed on child side of fork pre-exec` — `EXC_BAD_ACCESS` / SIGSEGV at `0x8`, single-threaded child. Symbolized:

```
os/exec.(*Cmd).CombinedOutput → Run → Start → os.StartProcess → os.startProcess
  → syscall.forkExec → syscall.forkAndExecInChild
    → syscall.rawSyscall
      → __tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl(__tsan::ThreadState*)   ← SIGSEGV
```

The forked child reaches the ThreadSanitizer runtime before it execs. TSan is not fork-safe — its trace buffer and locks were copied mid-flight from the multithreaded parent — so the child dies before the target binary (`entire`, `git`) ever runs. That's why there's no output.

`syscall.forkAndExecInChild` is `//go:norace`, and its comment justifies calling `rawSyscall` on the grounds that "they are assembly functions that do not grow the stack". True on Linux; **false on darwin**, where `rawSyscall`/`rawSyscall6`/`rawSyscall9` are ordinary Go functions wrapping libc trampolines, carrying `//go:nosplit` and `//go:uintptrkeepalive` but **not `//go:norace`**. Linux's `RawSyscall` has it, for exactly this reason:

> `//go:norace`, on RawSyscall, to avoid race instrumentation **if RawSyscall is called after fork**, or from a signal handler.

Known upstream: [golang/go#49138](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/49138), [#50172](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50172), [#50323](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/50323). Reproduced on go1.26.4 / macOS 26.6 / arm64.

Why it's rare and load-dependent: `TraceSwitchPartImpl` only runs when TSan's trace-buffer part boundary is hit, so it needs that boundary to land inside the child's handful of instrumented events.

## The fix

Skip `-race` for `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test` **on darwin only**.

**This costs no CI coverage.** CI runs `ubuntu-latest`, where the pragma exists and the crash cannot occur. The gate is `uname -s = Darwin`.

**And little local coverage**, because the package is overwhelmingly subprocess-driven: 272 of its 294 tests drive the spawned `entire` binary, which `TestMain` builds with a plain `go build` — no `-race`. So `-race` there can only instrument the *test harness*, never the CLI under test. Of the 22 in-process tests, most are harness self-tests (`TestTranscriptBuilder_*`, `TestNormalizeGitConfigForGuard_*`, `resolveHookCommandWithBinary`); the few that call production code directly (`agent.Get(...)` methods, `strategy.GetGitAuthorFromRepo`, the `TestLogin_*` flows) keep full race coverage on Linux, and their own packages are race-tested in `test:ci:core`.

## Shape of the change

- `mise-tasks/test/ci/integration/shard` — the one place the integration package's `go test` is invoked. Adds the darwin guard, with the full explanation and issue links in a comment, plus a line of output so it's visible when it applies.
- `test:ci` now delegates to the tasks CI actually runs (`test:ci:core` → integration shards `a`/`b`/`c` → canary) instead of its own `go test ./...`. This keeps the race decision in exactly one place and makes a local pass match CI. The shards partition the package exactly — 79 + 50 + 165 = 294, the full test count — so nothing is dropped.
- Extracted to `mise-tasks/test/ci/_default` (mirroring `mise-tasks/test/e2e/_default`) because `mise-tasks/lint/mise` rejects inline `run = """…"""` blocks of 3+ lines.
- `CLAUDE.md` documents why, so `-race` doesn't get helpfully re-added.

## Test plan

- `mise run test:ci` green end-to-end (core with `-race`, three shards, canary 59 + 4 tests).
- `mise run lint` clean, including `lint:mise` and `shellcheck`.
- Shard arithmetic verified against `go test -list`: a=79, b=50, c=165, total=294.
- Stability: three consecutive full passes over all three shards, **zero segfaults** (previously ~1 in 3 runs).
- Confirmed the guard is darwin-only — Linux still resolves to `go test -tags=integration -race …`.

## Follow-up worth considering

The real fix is upstream and tiny: add `//go:norace` to darwin's `rawSyscall`, `rawSyscall6`, `rawSyscall9` in `syscall/syscall_darwin.go`, matching Linux. Happy to file it.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)
EOF
)" 2>&1 | tail -3

**On your question — no, not all of them.** 272 of 294 tests drive the spawned binary; 22 run in-process. Those split into:

- **Harness self-tests** (`TestTranscriptBuilder_*` ×6, `TestNormalizeGitConfigForGuard_*` ×2, `resolveHookCommandWithBinary`) — testing this package's own helpers.
- **Real production code in-process** — `agent.Get(...)` methods, `strategy.GetGitAuthorFromRepo`, the four `TestLogin_*` flows against an httptest server.

So "disable `-race`, it covers nothing" would have been overclaiming. What made it safe anyway is something I'd missed earlier: **CI runs `ubuntu-latest`, where the `//go:norace` pragma exists and the crash cannot happen.** So the gate is darwin-only and CI coverage is untouched — those 22 tests keep full race coverage where it counts, and their own packages are race-tested in `test:ci:core` regardless.

The change:

- The guard lives in `mise-tasks/test/ci/integration/shard`, the single place that package's `go test` runs, with the mechanism and issue links in a comment and a visible log line when it applies.
- `test:ci` now delegates to the tasks CI actually runs (core → shards a/b/c → canary) rather than its own `go test ./...`, so the race decision has one home and a local pass matches CI. Verified the shards partition the package exactly: 79 + 50 + 165 = 294, the full test count.
- Extracted to `mise-tasks/test/ci/_default` — `mise-tasks/lint/mise` rejects inline `run` blocks of 3+ lines, which my first attempt tripped.
- `CLAUDE.md` records why, so `-race` doesn't get helpfully restored.

Verified: `mise run test:ci` green end-to-end, lint clean including `lint:mise` and shellcheck, and **three consecutive full passes over all shards with zero segfaults** (previously ~1 in 3).

Three PRs now: [#1897](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1897) multi-push-URL tests, [#1898](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1898) checkpoint_remote ownership, [#1899](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1899) this one. The upstream fix is still worth filing — three lines adding `//go:norace` to darwin's `rawSyscall*` — say the word and I'll write it up.

content.text:
Found it. Two separate facts, and neither is "the tests changed".

**1. The mechanism regressed in Go 1.26.0.** On Go ≤1.25, darwin's `rawSyscall` was a *bodiless declaration* backed by the runtime/assembly — the race detector cannot instrument a symbol that has no Go body, so the fork child never touched TSan and the crash was **impossible**. Go 1.26's `syscalln`/`rawsyscalln` refactor turned it into a real Go function, and nobody added the `//go:norace` that Linux's `RawSyscall` carries. That's also when the `exec_libc2.go` comment ("the calls to rawSyscall are okay because they are assembly functions") went stale for darwin — it used to be true there.

**2. This repo has been on Go 1.26 since February** — `b58ccebae`, 2026-02-22, *"update to go 1.26 (debug/buildinfo is a new default package)"*. So the crash has been *possible* for ~5 months, not new today.

**So why did nobody hit it?** Because almost nothing runs `-race` over that package. Only two commands in the whole repo do:

| Command | `-race`? | Exposed? |
|---|---|---|
| `mise run test` | no | no — doesn't even build the integration package |
| `mise run test:integration` | **no** | no |
| `mise run test:e2e` / `test:e2e:canary` | **no** | no |
| `test:ci:core` | yes | no — explicitly excludes the integration package |
| `mise run test:ci` / `mise run check` | yes | **yes, on macOS** |
| CI (`test:ci:integration:shard`) | yes | no — ubuntu, where the pragma exists |

Worth flagging since you said *e2e*: the e2e suite has **no `-race` anywhere**, so those runs could never have shown this. It's the integration package, and only through the full `test:ci`/`check` path.

That leaves exactly one exposed situation: a developer running the complete `mise run check` on a Mac. At ~1 in 3 per full run, a handful of those can easily come up clean — and I ran that path many times today validating three PRs, which is why it surfaced now rather than in February. CI, meanwhile, has never been able to see it.

I've updated the memory note with the Go 1.26 boundary and the exposure table, and added a "Why this only surfaced now" section to [#1899](https://github.com/entireio/cli/pull/1899) — it's the first thing a reviewer will ask, and "we've run these for months" is exactly the objection that needs answering in the PR itself.
I did run test:ci quite often and never saw it, yesterday in this session we saw it twice... with a 1/3 chance this is still somehow not making sense to me
Fair — 1/3 versus "often, never" doesn't reconcile. My rate estimate came from a handful of runs, so let me measure it properly and check what changed on the machine, not just in the repo.

---
name: integration-subprocess-segfault-flake
description: "Root cause + measured rates of intermittent 'signal: segmentation fault' from spawned subprocesses under -race on darwin: rawSyscall lacks //go:norace, so TSan runs in the fork child. Affects any fork-heavy package, often silently."
metadata:
  type: project
---

Under `-race` on **darwin**, a Go test that forks can die with `signal: segmentation fault`
in the child before `exec`. **Not our bug — a Go toolchain issue.**

**Root cause.** Crash report (`~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/*.ips`) says
`crashed on child side of fork pre-exec`, SIGSEGV at `0x8`, single-threaded child. Symbolized:

```
exec.Cmd.CombinedOutput → Run → Start → os.StartProcess → os.startProcess
  → syscall.forkExec → syscall.forkAndExecInChild → syscall.rawSyscall
    → __tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl(__tsan::ThreadState*)   ← SIGSEGV
```

`forkAndExecInChild` is `//go:norace` and justifies calling rawSyscall because "they are
assembly functions". **Was true on darwin until Go 1.26**, which turned `rawSyscall` from a
bodiless runtime/assembly declaration into a real Go function (`rawsyscalln` refactor) —
without adding the `//go:norace` that Linux's `RawSyscall` carries explicitly "to avoid race
instrumentation if RawSyscall is called after fork". Verified by diffing
`syscall/syscall_darwin.go` between go1.25.6 (no body) and go1.26.0+ (body).
Upstream: golang/go#49138, #50172, #50323.

**Measured rates** (2026-08-05, quiet Mac Studio, macOS 26.6, go1.26.4):

| Command | Crash rate |
|---|---|
| single package `-race` (`./cmd/entire/cli/integration_test/`) | 0 / 8 runs |
| `go test -tags=integration -race ./...` | 1 / 4 runs |

`./...` runs many race-instrumented package binaries concurrently, which is the amplifier.
An earlier "~1 in 3" estimate was a small-sample artifact — do not quote it.

**It is often SILENT.** A fork-child crash only fails the suite when it lands on a subprocess
call whose error is checked; best-effort paths swallow it. Proven: a crash report at
2026-08-04 21:50 belongs to a `./...` run that exited 0 with no "segmentation fault" text
anywhere. So this has plausibly been happening since the Go 1.26 bump (repo moved
2026-02-22, `b58ccebae`) while only rarely being *visible* — which is why nobody reported it.

**Not confined to the integration package.** A reproduction landed in
`cmd/entire/cli/strategy` (`TestReconcileDisconnected_ModifiedEntries`, `git commit` fork) —
that package has ~153 exec call sites. Any fork-heavy race-instrumented package is exposed.

**Mitigation in tree:** `-race` is off for `cmd/entire/cli/integration_test` on darwin
(`mise-tasks/test/ci/integration/shard`) — that package is ~272/294 subprocess-driven and the
spawned binary is built without `-race`, so `-race` there only ever instrumented the harness.
Packages like `strategy` keep `-race` (they have real in-process concurrency) and stay exposed
on darwin. CI is Linux, immune.

**Caveat when investigating:** `.ips` retention here is only ~4 days and `Retired/` is empty,
so absence of old crash reports proves nothing about the past.

Distinct from [[go-git-reconcile-flake]] (go-git "object not found", not a segfault).
See also [[git-stash-untracked-pitfall]].

You're right to push back — my 1/3 was wrong, and chasing the discrepancy turned up better answers.

## Corrected rates (today, quiet machine, same OS + Go)

| Command | Crashes |
|---|---|
| single package `-race` | **0 / 8** |
| `go test -tags=integration -race ./...` | **1 / 4** |

"~1 in 3" was a small-sample artifact of yesterday's mixed runs. The amplifier is running *many* race-instrumented package binaries concurrently — which is exactly what the old `./...`-shaped `test:ci` did, and not what my 8 single-package runs did.

## The real reason you never saw it: it's usually silent

A fork-child crash only fails the suite when it lands on a subprocess call whose error is actually checked. Best-effort paths swallow it. Proof: yesterday's third crash report (21:50:19) belongs to a `./...` run that **exited 0 with zero "segmentation fault" text anywhere in its output**. The crash happened, macOS wrote the report, and the suite passed clean.

So this has plausibly been happening since the repo moved to Go 1.26 in February — just almost never *visibly*. What was unusual yesterday wasn't the machine, it was me: I ran the full race suite ~14 times back-to-back validating three PRs, which is far more sampling than a normal day, so I drew three visible hits instead of zero.

## It's not confined to the integration package

Today's reproduction failed in **`cmd/entire/cli/strategy`** — `TestReconcileDisconnected_ModifiedEntries`, on a `git commit` fork. That package has ~153 exec call sites. Any fork-heavy race-instrumented package is exposed on darwin, so **#1899 is not a complete darwin fix**. I've deliberately left `strategy` alone: unlike the integration package, it has real in-process concurrency worth race-testing. The PR takes only the case where `-race` is pure cost and leaves the rest to the upstream one-liner. I've updated the PR body to say this explicitly rather than let a reviewer infer the flake is now gone.

## On the macOS theory — weaker than it looked

macOS 26.6 did land yesterday 08:37 with CLT at 09:36, and all three crashes were 20:28–21:50 the same day. But it's correlation I can't prove: today is also 26.6 and reproduces at 1/4, Go has been on 1.26 since February, and — importantly — `.ips` retention here is only ~4 days with `Retired/` empty, so the absence of older crash reports proves nothing about the past. I'd stopped short of verifying that before, which is what made the OS story look stronger than the evidence supports.

Net: mechanism proven, rate corrected, "why now" is mostly **sampling volume plus a normally-silent failure**, not a step change.

input.content:
# syscall: on darwin, rawSyscall lacks //go:norace, so race instrumentation runs in the fork child and can crash it before exec

### Go version

`go version go1.26.4 darwin/arm64` (`CGO_ENABLED=1`)

Present in go1.26.0 through go1.26.5. **Not** present in go1.25.x — see Analysis.

Host: macOS 26.6 (25G72), arm64.

### What did you do?

Ran a large race-instrumented test suite on darwin in which most tests spawn subprocesses
(`os/exec`), i.e. `go test -race ./...` over a tree where one package shells out to `git` and
to a built binary hundreds of times.

### What did you expect to see?

The child process `exec`s the target binary, or `cmd.Run()` returns an ordinary error.

### What did you see instead?

Intermittently, the forked child dies with SIGSEGV **before it execs**. To the Go program this
surfaces as:

```
signal: segmentation fault
```

from `cmd.Run()` / `cmd.CombinedOutput()`, with **empty** child output — the target binary
never runs. There is no Go panic and no race report.

The macOS crash report (`~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/<binary>-*.ips`) identifies it
precisely:

```
"asi": { "libsystem_c.dylib": ["crashed on child side of fork pre-exec"] }
exception: EXC_BAD_ACCESS (SIGSEGV), KERN_INVALID_ADDRESS at 0x0000000000000008
threadCount: 1        (the forked child, as expected)
procName / parentProc: <test binary>
```

Symbolized faulting thread (frames all resolve inside the statically linked test binary,
because the TSan runtime is linked in):

```
__tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl(__tsan::ThreadState*)     <-- SIGSEGV
syscall.rawSyscall
syscall.forkAndExecInChild
syscall.forkExec
os.startProcess
os.StartProcess
os/exec.(*Cmd).Start
os/exec.(*Cmd).Run
os/exec.(*Cmd).CombinedOutput
```

### Analysis

`syscall.forkAndExecInChild` (`src/syscall/exec_libc2.go`, used by darwin) is `//go:norace`,
and documents why that is sufficient:

```go
// In the child, this function must not acquire any locks, because
// they might have been locked at the time of the fork. This means
// no rescheduling, no malloc calls, and no new stack segments.
// For the same reason compiler does not race instrument it.
// The calls to rawSyscall are okay because they are assembly
// functions that do not grow the stack.
//
//go:norace
func forkAndExecInChild(...)
```

Its body calls `rawSyscall` 26 times and `rawSyscall6` once.

**That invariant held on darwin through Go 1.25 and no longer holds.** In go1.25.6,
`src/syscall/syscall_darwin.go` declared them with no Go body:

```go
// Implemented in the runtime package (runtime/sys_darwin.go)
func syscall(fn, a1, a2, a3 uintptr) (r1, r2 uintptr, err Errno)
func rawSyscall(fn, a1, a2, a3 uintptr) (r1, r2 uintptr, err Errno)
```

In go1.26 (the `syscalln`/`rawsyscalln` refactor) they became ordinary Go functions:

```go
//go:linkname rawSyscall
//go:nosplit
//go:uintptrkeepalive
func rawSyscall(fn, a1, a2, a3 uintptr) (r1, r2 uintptr, err Errno) {
	r1, r2, err = rawsyscalln(fn, a1, a2, a3)
	return r1, r2, errno(r1, err)
}
```

`//go:nosplit` and `//go:uintptrkeepalive` are present; **`//go:norace` is not**. So under
`-race` the compiler instruments `rawSyscall`, and the fork child calls into the TSan runtime
before `exec` — where TSan's per-thread trace state was copied from a multithreaded parent and
is not safe to touch. `TraceSwitchPartImpl` (trace-part rotation) is where it faults.

Linux already guards exactly this hazard, and names it (`src/syscall/syscall_linux.go`):

```go
// //go:norace, on RawSyscall, to avoid race instrumentation if RawSyscall is
// called after fork, or from a signal handler.

//go:uintptrkeepalive
//go:nosplit
//go:norace
//go:linkname RawSyscall
func RawSyscall(trap, a1, a2, a3 uintptr) (r1, r2 uintptr, err Errno) {
```

On darwin, none of `syscall`, `syscall6`, `syscall9`, `rawSyscall`, `rawSyscall6`,
`rawSyscall9` carry `//go:norace`, and all now have Go bodies.

**Scope appears to be darwin only.** The other libc-based `forkAndExecInChild`
(`src/syscall/exec_libc.go`, aix/solaris) still relies on `raw*` helpers that are declared
without Go bodies (`rawSyscall6` in `syscall_aix.go`, `rawSysvicall6` in `syscall_solaris.go`),
so they are not instrumentable and are unaffected.

### Why it is intermittent

`TraceSwitchPartImpl` only runs when the thread's TSan trace part fills, so the crash requires
the forking thread's trace position to be near a part boundary at fork time. Observed rates in
a real suite (quiet machine, go1.26.4, macOS 26.6):

| Command | Crash rate |
|---|---|
| `go test -race` over one fork-heavy package | 0 / 8 runs |
| `go test -race ./...` (many race-instrumented package binaries concurrently) | 1 / 4 runs |

It is also frequently **silent**: the fork child crashes and macOS writes a report, but the
suite still exits 0, because the failure is only observable if that particular caller checks
the error from `exec`. We have one crash report that belongs to a run which passed with no
mention of a segfault anywhere in its output. This likely makes the problem considerably more
common than the reported-failure rate suggests.

### Suggested fix

Add `//go:norace` to `rawSyscall` and `rawSyscall6` in `src/syscall/syscall_darwin.go` (the two
reached from `forkAndExecInChild`); for consistency `rawSyscall9` as well, and possibly the
non-raw variants given the signal-handler half of the Linux rationale.

The stale comment in `src/syscall/exec_libc2.go` ("The calls to rawSyscall are okay because
they are assembly functions that do not grow the stack") should also be corrected, since it is
what makes the current state look intentional.

### Reproducer

We were unable to reduce this to a small self-contained program: a fork storm with concurrent
instrumented memory traffic (including instrumented work on the forking goroutine itself, to
sweep trace-part boundary offsets) did not reproduce it in several attempts. The window is
narrow and appears to need a substantial race-instrumented working set plus several concurrent
race-instrumented processes.

Practical reproduction: a large race-instrumented test suite whose tests spawn subprocesses,
run repeatedly with `go test -race ./...`, watching for `signal: segmentation fault` from
`cmd.Run()` **and** for new `*.ips` crash reports in
`~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/` (the silent case).

### Related issues

Same symptom reported on macOS against older Go releases, without this root cause identified:
#49138, #50172, #50323.

## The issue in one paragraph

`syscall.forkAndExecInChild` (darwin's `exec_libc2.go`) is `//go:norace` and justifies calling `rawSyscall` from the fork child on the grounds that "they are assembly functions". **That was true on darwin through Go 1.25 and stopped being true in Go 1.26**: the `syscalln`/`rawsyscalln` refactor turned `rawSyscall` into an ordinary Go function with a body, carrying `//go:nosplit` and `//go:uintptrkeepalive` but **not** `//go:norace`. So under `-race` the child calls into TSan between `fork` and `exec` — where its per-thread trace state was copied from a multithreaded parent — and intermittently dies at `__tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl` with SIGSEGV at `0x8`.

## Why it's a strong report

- **Linux already fixes exactly this**, with the hazard named in the comment: `RawSyscall` carries `//go:norace` "to avoid race instrumentation if RawSyscall is called after fork, or from a signal handler." Darwin's equivalents have no such pragma.
- **Version boundary proven by source diff**: go1.25.6 declares `rawSyscall` with no body ("Implemented in the runtime package"); go1.26.0+ gives it one.
- **Scope is precise**: `forkAndExecInChild` calls `rawSyscall` 26× and `rawSyscall6` 1×. The other libc-based platforms (aix/solaris, `exec_libc.go`) still use bodiless `raw*` declarations, so **darwin is the only affected platform**.
- **Symptom is unambiguous**: crash report says `crashed on child side of fork pre-exec`, single-threaded child, and the symbolized stack runs `CombinedOutput → … → forkAndExecInChild → rawSyscall → __tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl`.

## Two things I flagged honestly rather than glossed

**No minimal reproducer.** I tried twice, including targeting the forking goroutine's own trace position to sweep part boundaries — didn't reproduce. The window needs a large instrumented working set plus several concurrent race-instrumented processes. The report says so and gives the practical reproduction instead, which is the honest position and better than shipping a repro that doesn't fire.

**The silent case is probably the bigger deal.** A fork-child crash only becomes a visible failure if that particular caller checks the `exec` error; otherwise the suite passes and only an `.ips` file records it. I have one crash report belonging to a run that exited 0 with no segfault text anywhere. That's worth emphasizing to the Go team because it means the real incidence is likely well above the reported-failure rate — and it's why nobody on your team noticed for five months.

Suggested fix is three lines: `//go:norace` on `rawSyscall`/`rawSyscall6` (plus `rawSyscall9` for consistency), and correct the now-misleading comment in `exec_libc2.go` so the current state doesn't keep reading as intentional.

---
name: integration-subprocess-segfault-flake
description: "Intermittent SIGSEGV from spawned subprocesses under -race on darwin was a Go bug fixed in go1.26.5 (rawSyscall missing //go:norace). Fix = bump the Go pin, not a test workaround."
metadata:
  type: project
---

Under `-race` on **darwin**, a Go test that forks could die with `signal: segmentation fault` in
the child before `exec`. **Go toolchain bug, FIXED IN go1.26.5** (released 2026-07-01).

**Root cause.** Go 1.26 turned darwin's `syscall.rawSyscall` from a bodiless
runtime/assembly declaration into a real Go function (`rawsyscalln` refactor) without adding
`//go:norace`. `syscall.forkAndExecInChild` is `//go:norace` and justified calling rawSyscall
because "they are assembly functions" — true on darwin until 1.26. So under `-race` the fork
child ran TSan instrumentation and faulted in `__tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl` (null ThreadState
field deref, SIGSEGV at `0x8`). Upstream: golang/go#79804, CL 786620, 1.26 backport #79806.

**The fix, verifiable locally:**
`diff ~/.local/share/mise/installs/go/1.26.{4,5}/src/syscall/syscall_darwin.go`
→ 1.26.5 adds `//go:norace` to `rawSyscall`, `rawSyscall6`, `rawSyscall9`, `errno`, `errnoX`,
`errnoPtr`, and corrects the `exec_libc2.go` comment. **So: bump the Go pin (mise.toml +
go.mod) rather than disabling `-race`.** Affected range is go1.26.0–1.26.4 only.

**Diagnostics that worked** (reuse for any "spawned subprocess segfaulted" report):
`~/Library/Logs/DiagnosticReports/<binary>-*.ips` — look for
`asi: ["crashed on child side of fork pre-exec"]`, `threadCount: 1`, `procName == parentProc`.
Symbolize `imageOffset` + `0x100000000` against a rebuild. **Go test binaries here are
bit-reproducible** (same commit → same LC_UUID) and **std-lib symbol addresses are invariant to
repo-code changes**, so std frames symbolize reliably even from a non-matching build — but
repo-code frames resolve to visible nonsense, so never trust those without a UUID match.
`go tool objdump` the suspect function to confirm instrumentation is really present.

**Mistakes made diagnosing it — don't repeat:**
- Did not `diff` the newer Go already installed on disk, nor search upstream for the `.ips`
  annotation string. Both would have found the shipped fix in one step, before writing a
  duplicate bug report.
- Claimed "the frame chain reads coherently, so the mapping must be right". Unsound — near-miss
  builds yield plausible-but-wrong chains. Establish build determinism and std-layout
  invariance instead.
- Paired a crash report to a test run without checking `procLaunch`/`captureTime` against the
  log's mtime, and wrongly concluded crashes were "often silent" (they were 17 min apart).
  Zero silent instances were ever demonstrated.
- Quoted a "~1 in 3" rate from a handful of runs; measured later as 0/8 (single package) and
  1/4 (`./...`), n far too small for the mechanism claims built on it.
- Missed one of four crash reports present in the same directory.

`.ips` retention here is only ~4 days and `Retired/` is empty, so absence of old reports proves
nothing. ReportCrash also throttles duplicates — a reproduced crash produced no new `.ips`.

Distinct from [[go-git-reconcile-flake]] (go-git "object not found", not a segfault).
See also [[git-stash-untracked-pitfall]].

## What

Bumps the Go pin from 1.26.4 to **1.26.5** in `mise.toml` and `go.mod`. 1.26.5 is the current stable release, and it fixes a Go bug that made `go test -race` intermittently fail on darwin with `signal: segmentation fault` from a spawned subprocess.

## The bug it fixes

The child of `fork()` crashed **before it could exec**, so the target binary (`git`, or the built `entire` CLI) never ran and produced no output. No Go panic, no race report — a different test hit each run, indistinguishable from a real regression in whatever you were working on.

Go 1.26 turned darwin's `syscall.rawSyscall` from a bodiless runtime/assembly declaration into an ordinary Go function, without adding `//go:norace`. `syscall.forkAndExecInChild` is `//go:norace` and justified calling `rawSyscall` from the fork child on the grounds that *"they are assembly functions"* — true on darwin until 1.26. So under `-race` the child ran TSan instrumentation and faulted:

```
os/exec.(*Cmd).CombinedOutput → Run → Start → os.StartProcess → os.startProcess
  → syscall.forkExec → syscall.forkAndExecInChild → syscall.rawSyscall
    → __tsan::TraceSwitchPartImpl(__tsan::ThreadState*)   ← SIGSEGV at 0x8
```

macOS crash reports confirm it directly: `asi: ["crashed on child side of fork pre-exec"]`, `EXC_BAD_ACCESS`, single-threaded child.

Upstream: [golang/go#79804](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/79804), 1.26 backport [#79806](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/79806). 1.26.5 adds `//go:norace` to `rawSyscall`, `rawSyscall6`, `rawSyscall9` and the `errno`/`errnoX`/`errnoPtr` helpers, and corrects the stale comment. Verifiable without leaving your machine:

```bash

     $(mise where go@1.26.5)/src/syscall/syscall_darwin.go
```

## Scope

Affected range is **go1.26.0 – 1.26.4**, so this repo was exposed from the 1.26 bump (`b58ccebae`, 2026-02-22) until now. **darwin only**: Linux's `RawSyscall` has carried `//go:norace` all along (with a comment naming this exact hazard), and the other libc-based platforms (aix, solaris) still declare their `raw*` helpers without Go bodies, so nothing there is instrumentable. CI runs `ubuntu-latest` and was never affected.

Confirmed — exactly as you describe. Both from the code and from the test:

```
[entire] Pushing 1 checkpoint ref(s) to origin...
[entire] Some checkpoint refs diverged; syncing 1 ref(s) individually... pushed 0 of 1
fatal: '…/does-not-exist.git' does not appear to be a git repository
```

## The mechanism

`batchPushRefs` issues **one** `git push <remote-name> <refspecs…>`. Because the target is the remote *name*, git fans out to every push URL inside that single process, and any URL failing makes the whole invocation exit non-zero. So:

- `queue.Remove(existing)` sits behind `if batchErr == nil` — a partial failure removes **nothing**, not even the refs that landed.
- The per-ref recovery can't rescue it either: `pushCheckpointRefWithRecovery` runs `git push <remote-name>` for one ref, which fans out again, so it still hits the broken URL. `pushed` stays empty (`pushed 0 of 1`), and `Remove(pushed)` early-returns on `len(refs) == 0`.

We have no way to isolate a single URL, and the queue has no per-destination state to record it with — entries are `{"ref": …}` only.

## Two consequences worth being explicit about

**The refs did land on the healthy URL.** The test asserts that: `CheckpointExistsOnRemote(bareA, checkpointID)` passes while the ref stays queued. So the queue retains refs that are already present on some remotes. That's safe — the retry is idempotent, the healthy URL just reports up-to-date — but it means **the queue never drains while any push URL is broken.** A permanently dead mirror gives you a permanently non-empty queue, retried on every push, visible only on stderr. That's the "degrades toward will-retry, never toward silent loss" property working as designed, with that as the price.

**One diagnosability wart I noticed re-reading the output:** the recovery message hardcodes `"Some checkpoint refs diverged; syncing …"` regardless of *why* the batch failed. Here the cause was an unreachable URL, and the user is told their refs diverged. Cosmetic, but actively misleading for exactly the multi-URL case — worth a small follow-up to phrase it by cause (or neutrally) since divergence and unreachability want different user actions. content.text:
That proposal has a problem I'd want to flag before building it — and checking it turned up a pre-existing bug.

## The read side is pinned to the *fetch* URL

`FetchCheckpointRef` → `checkpointFetchTarget` (`checkpoint_ref.go:44`) → `fetchURLAuthoritative`, which reads `git remote get-url origin` — i.e. **`url[0]`**, never a pushurl. So if refs are pushed to `pushurl[0]`:

- **no `pushurl` configured** → `pushurl[0] == url[0]`. Push and read agree. Fine.
- **`pushurl` configured** → we'd write to `pushurl[0]` and read from `url[0]`, two different repos. The checkpoints become unreadable from any other clone. It still works locally only because the local ref is retained after push — so the split stays invisible until someone clones or resumes elsewhere, which is exactly when checkpoints matter.

Picking `url[0]` instead doesn't rescue it: a `pushurl` usually exists *because* `url` isn't writable (fetch upstream, push fork), so we'd be pushing session data at a repo we have no write access to.

So neither single-URL choice derived from the remote is coherent. The only coherent single destination is one used for **both** directions — which is what `checkpoint_remote` already is (`PushURL` and `FetchURL` both resolve it). That means for the "I don't want checkpoints everywhere" need, there may be nothing to build: the mechanism exists, and it keeps the principle we settled on for branch — a single destination comes from explicit config, never inferred from topology. Now with a mechanical reason, not just a philosophical one.

## The pre-existing bug this exposes

Today, with any `pushurl` set, refs are pushed to the pushurl repos while reads fetch from `url[0]` — so **a second clone already cannot hydrate them.** Your proposal wouldn't cause that; it just wouldn't fix it. It's squarely in #1897's topic and currently untested. I'd add a test for it (clone from `url[0]`, assert the checkpoint is unreachable) so the gap is pinned rather than folklore.

## What I'd actually build for the queue problem

If the goal is "a broken mirror shouldn't wedge the queue forever", the fix is **per-destination queue entries** — `{ref, destination}` instead of `{ref}`, drained and removed per URL. That keeps fan-out (so mirror users keep working, and reads keep resolving), and a dead mirror retains only its own entries. Cost: a queue format change and N pushes instead of one fan-out push. The fast-forward-only impossibility we hit on the branch backend barely bites here, since per-checkpoint refs only diverge if a backfill or migration rewrote the same checkpoint ID.

So my recommendation: **keep fan-out, make the queue per-destination, and leave single-destination to `checkpoint_remote`.**

That said — if you still want refs to go to one URL only, I'll build it, but then the read side has to move with it or we're shipping a write-only store. Which way do you want it?
one more question on how git works: if multiple urls are configured for a single remote and one of them fails during push, it continues with the ones coming after?

Answer: **it depends on the failure mode**, and the difference matters for us.

| First URL fails with… | Later URLs | Exit | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ref rejection** (non-fast-forward) | ✅ still pushed | 1 | `push_with_options` returns error → `errs++` → loop continues |
| **transport failure** (unreachable, auth, no such repo) | ❌ **skipped entirely** | 128 | `die()` — process exits inside `transport_get`/connect, never returns to the loop |

Case 2 output shows it plainly — `reject.git` rejected, and `good2.git` still got `* [new branch]`:

```
To ../reject.git
 ! [rejected]        HEAD -> main (non-fast-forward)
To ../good2.git
 * [new branch]      HEAD -> main
exit=1
```

Case 1, unreachable first:
```
fatal: '../MISSING.git' does not appear to be a git repository
exit=128
good.git got the ref? NO
```

So the `errs++`-no-`break` loop in `builtin/push.c:438` only describes the *recoverable* path. `die()` on a transport failure never reaches the accumulator.

## Why this matters for #1897 and the queue design

My earlier test put the unreachable URL **second**, so the healthy one had already been pushed and I concluded "refs land on the reachable URL and stay queued". **That conclusion is order-dependent and I stated it too broadly.** With the dead mirror listed *first*:

- checkpoint refs reach **nothing** — not even the healthy URL;
- the queue correctly retains everything (so no loss);
- but every subsequent push also dies at URL 1, so a single dead mirror in first position **blocks checkpoint sync entirely**, indefinitely, while the user's own branch pushes fail too (exit 128 is hard to miss, at least).

It also sharpens the per-destination-queue idea I recommended: pushing per URL rather than relying on fan-out would make a dead first mirror stop blocking the others — which is an argument *for* that design beyond just queue bookkeeping.

I'd add a second unreachable-URL test to #1897 with the bad URL **first**, asserting nothing reaches the healthy URL — that's the worse case and it's currently undocumented. Want me to add it, and fix the doc comment on the existing test to say the position was deliberate?

**My "write-only store" worry was overstated.** Walking it through properly: on the same machine the local ref still exists, so no fetch happens and read routing is irrelevant. A clone of `pushurl[0]` has that repo as *its* `url[0]`, so reads resolve there correctly. A clone of some other mirror finds nothing — but that's true today too. So the model is coherent and needs no read-side change: **checkpoints live in exactly one repo; clone that repo and reads work.**

One thing your inference doesn't cover, worth stating since it's the real trade: a *rejecting* first URL (non-fast-forward) does **not** block the others today, so under fan-out refs still reach mirrors 2..N. First-URL-only gives that up. Equivalent for the transport case, strictly less resilient for the rejection case, in exchange for a single deterministic destination. The push-discovery queue records only a ref — `{"ref": …}`, no per-destination state — so *"this ref is pushed"* has to mean one place. git's fan-out across a remote's several push URLs can't provide that, in two distinct ways:

The multi-remote case is worth saying out loud independently: checkpoints follow whichever remote you push to, while `resume`/`explain` always read via `origin`, so checkpoints pushed elsewhere aren't found again.

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change is implemented at the right depth, not as a fragile
bandaid. Special cases layered on shared infrastructure are a sign the fix
isn't deep enough — prefer generalizing the underlying mechanism over adding
special cases.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than

content.text:
Done. Four agents, findings deduped, fixes applied and pushed to #1905.

## Fixed — real problems, not style

**The efficiency finding was the valuable one.** I'd put `resolveRefsPushDestination` (and its `git remote get-url --push --all` spawn) *before* `flushCheckpointRefsQueue`'s early returns, so **every** push on the default backend paid a fork/exec for a destination that goes unused when nothing is queued — and multi-URL users got the warning on no-op pushes. Now resolved after both early returns, inside the existing perf span. That's an intended behavior change: no more warning on an empty-queue push.

**Two divergences in what we tell users**, both caught by altitude:
- Doctor treated `checkpoint_remote` *present in settings* as pinned and went silent — but `PushURL` only honors it when it resolves (owner mismatch, unparseable URL, non-derivable protocol all fall back), so doctor stayed quiet while pushes really went first-URL-only. Now asks `remote.PushURL` per remote — the "ask the client, don't re-resolve" rule CLAUDE.md documents for `CoreOrigin()`, which I'd violated.
- It reported the first *sorted* fanning-out remote, so a repo with a fanning-out `backup` it never pushes to got warned about a rule that didn't apply. Now per-remote and named.

**Two things I'd written that were already wrong:** the git-branch explanation described the *refs* failure behavior, and `display` claimed "checkpoint remote" for a self-picked URL while the same struct's `checkpointRemote` said false.

**Dedup:** "redact if URL-shaped else pass the path through" existed in three copies — two mine, one pre-existing in `redactGitArgs`. Now one `gitremote.RedactURLOrPath`. Test helpers collapsed onto one `setPushURLs(remote, urls...)` primitive with position as the parameter. `display` became a method, resolver branches 5→3, the two print wrappers became one, `indent` and the `io.Writer` param (both single-valued) gone, doctor subtests table-driven. N+1 subprocesses in the topology inspector became one `git remote -v`.

Also fixed both file headers still claiming the CLI "has no per-URL control" — true only for git-branch now.

## Two corrections to the agents

**The orphaned `checkCodexHookTrust` doc was pre-existing**, not caused by my insert — two agents attributed it to me; `git show` on the base branch shows it already detached. Fixed anyway (zero-risk comment move), but described accurately in the commit.

**Skipped:** altitude's largest finding — refactor `pushSettings.pushTarget()` to return a typed destination and change `displayPushTarget`/`printCheckpointRemoteHint`/`printProtectedRefBlock` signatures, which would also fix the pre-existing "checkpoint remote" mislabel on the git-branch path for bare-URL pushes. It's the right end state, but it rewrites pre-existing behavior across both backends — too much for this PR. I fixed only the inconsistency I introduced. Worth its own PR.

## One incidental confirmation

`mise run check` failed once with `signal: segmentation fault` on `git init --bare` — the darwin `-race` fork-child bug, because this branch is stacked on main and doesn't carry the Go 1.26.5 bump. Re-ran the same packages under 1.26.5: clean. Then `mise run check` green on the retry, lint 0 issues, canary 59 + 4. Another reason to land #1904 early.

Fixed and pushed.

## The Entire trail finding — it's on **#1898**, not this PR

Trail 971, medium severity, confidence 0.55, at `checkpoint/remote/util.go:342`:

> `checkpointRemoteIsInherited` now treats a missing `origin` remote as automatically "inherited" (falls back, disabling `checkpoint_remote`), whereas the previous check was based on the actual push remote's owner and didn't require an `origin` remote to exist at all. A repo that pushes via a remote whose owner matches the configured `checkpoint_remote` owner, but has no remote literally named `origin`, will now silently lose checkpoint-remote routing even though the old code would have used it. This path isn't covered by any test in `util_test.go`.

**I traced it and it's correct.** Old code read the push remote's URL and compared *its* owner, so a repo whose only remote is `upstream` (same owner as the checkpoint repo) kept checkpoint-remote routing. My version returns `inherited` as soon as `originURL == ""`, before the push remote is ever consulted — so that topology silently loses its configured destination. And the coverage claim holds: the nearest existing cases are "no checkpoint remote + origin missing" and "missing push remote + origin present", neither of which hits this combination.

The fix keeps the origin-first rule intact: when origin exists it decides, and only when origin is *absent* fall back to the push remote's owner as the sole available identity signal — which is what the old code effectively did, and with no origin there's no origin-vs-push-remote divergence to worry about anyway. Plus the test case that was missing.

Trail 979 on this branch has zero findings, and trail 970 on #1897 (tests-only) also zero.

## Also worth knowing

**Trail 978 reports `merged` — PR #1904 (Go 1.26.5) landed.** That explains the `-race` segfault I hit during the simplify verification: this branch is stacked on `soph/multi-pushurl-tests`, which is based on main from *before* that merge, so it's still pinned to 1.26.4. Rebasing #1897 onto current main will carry the bump down the stack.

Also visible in the trail list: `git-refs-as-default-backend` is merged — "Make git-refs the sole enable default; drop backend picker". That makes #1905's destination rule apply to every new repo rather than an opt-in backend, which raises its stakes a little.

git add -A && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
fix(checkpoint): keep checkpoint_remote when a repo has no origin

Entire trail finding (trail 971, medium): checkpointRemoteIsInherited treated a
missing origin remote as automatically inherited, so it fell back and disabled
checkpoint_remote. The predecessor compared the *push remote's* owner and never
required a remote literally named origin, so a repo whose only remote is e.g.
"upstream" — with an owner matching the configured checkpoint repo — silently
lost checkpoint-remote routing under the new check.

Origin still decides when it exists. It is only when there is no origin at all
that the push remote serves as the identity, which is what the old code
effectively did; in that topology there is no origin-vs-push-remote divergence to
worry about, because the repo has exactly one identity.

The check therefore moves after the push-remote read (needed for transport
anyway) so that URL is available as the fallback identity. The reason strings now
name which remote was consulted.

Two test cases, both verified to fail against the previous logic (the first
reported `enabled = false, want true`):
  - no origin + same-owner push remote -> checkpoint remote kept
  - no origin + differently-owned push remote -> still reads as inherited

TestPushURL gains //nolint:maintidx: the score tracks the size of the case table,
not branching logic, matching the existing convention in this repo.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
EOF
